lesson.title: Gear trains: speed and torque

lead.text: A bicycle's gears are wheels with teeth cut around the rim. Each one is fixed to a shaft, a rod that turns along with it. When two gears mesh, the teeth of one slot between the teeth of the other, so as one turns it pushes the other round. The gear you turn is the driver, and the gear it pushes is the driven gear.

Gear speeds are given in rpm, which stands for revolutions per minute: a gear at 60 rpm turns once every second. The teeth cannot slip, so the two gears must pass teeth at the same rate where they touch. Take a driver with 20 teeth that makes one full turn. Twenty teeth go past the contact point, so twenty teeth of the driven gear go past too. If the driven gear also has 20 teeth, that is a whole turn for it as well. If it has 40 teeth, twenty of them are only half a turn.

afterFigure.text: So the gear with more teeth turns more slowly, and the gear with fewer teeth turns faster. Multiply each gear's speed by its number of teeth and you get the same answer for both: in the second pair, 600 × 20 for the driver and 300 × 40 for the driven gear are both 12,000. Engineers describe a pair by its gear ratio, the driven gear's teeth divided by the driver's teeth. Here that is 40 ÷ 20 = 2, and the driven gear turns at the driver's speed divided by 2.

lead.text: Count the teeth that pass the contact point in one turn of the driver. The figure shows two pairs, and only one of them matches the question.

A pair of gears changes the speed, and it changes how hard the output shaft pushes as well. That needs a word. The turning effect of a force on a shaft is its torque, found like a moment: the force times its distance from the axis. A pedal pushed with 100 N at 0.2 m from the axle gives a torque of 100 × 0.2 = 20 N·m.

The second idea is power, the energy delivered each second. A turning shaft delivers more power the larger its torque and the faster it turns, so doubling either one doubles the power. Now take an ideal mesh, one whose teeth waste no energy. Whatever power goes into the driver comes out of the driven gear, so torque × speed has to be the same on both.

afterFigure.text: That settles the trade. If the driven gear turns at half the speed, its torque must be double. A 20-tooth driver delivering 10 N·m to a 40-tooth gear passes on a shaft that turns at half the speed with 20 N·m. Slow the shaft down by any factor and the torque rises by the same factor. It is the lever bargain again: the lever gave a bigger force over a shorter distance, and a gear pair gives a bigger torque at a lower speed.

lead.text: The mesh keeps the power the same. Decide what must happen to the torque when the speed falls.

steps.headline: A 24-tooth driver turns at 600 rpm and supplies 8 N·m to a 72-tooth gear. The mesh is lossless. Find the output speed and torque.

lead.text: Two gears that mesh push on each other at the contact point, and that reverses the turning. Where the driver's rim moves down, the driven gear's rim moves up, so one turns clockwise while the other turns anticlockwise. Sometimes you want the output to turn the same way as the input. Sometimes the two shafts sit too far apart for the gears to meet.

The fix is a third gear between them, called an idler. It meshes with the driver on one side and with the output gear on the other. The idler turns against the driver, and the output turns against the idler, which sends the output round in the same direction as the driver.

afterFigure.text: The idler's speed follows the usual rule against the driver, and then its tooth count cancels out of the final answer. Take a 24-tooth driver at 600 rpm with a 36-tooth idler and a 48-tooth output. The idler turns at 600 × 24 ÷ 36 = 400 rpm, and the output turns at 400 × 36 ÷ 48 = 300 rpm. Without the idler, 600 × 24 ÷ 48 is also 300 rpm. An idler changes which way the output turns and how far apart the shafts sit. It leaves the speed ratio alone.

lead.text: The idler meshes directly with the driver, so the output gear does not come into this part of the problem.

A bicycle does not mesh its gears directly. The pedals turn a large toothed wheel, the chainring, and a chain carries the motion to a small toothed wheel on the back wheel, the sprocket. The chain's links fit over the teeth of both wheels, so it carries teeth past each of them at the same rate, just as a mesh does. The rule is the same as before: speed × teeth is equal on both.

The direction is different. A chain loops from one wheel to the other and reverses nothing, so both turn the same way. Suppose the chainring has 40 teeth and the sprocket has 20, with the pedals turning at 50 rpm. The sprocket is driven and has half the teeth, so it turns at 50 × 40 ÷ 20 = 100 rpm.

This is what the gear lever on a bicycle does. It moves the chain between sprockets of different sizes at the back. A large sprocket turns the back wheel slowly with a high torque, which suits a hill. A small one turns it fast with less torque, which suits the flat.

Sometimes a machine needs a big change of speed. A motor turning at 1,500 rpm may have to drive a drum at 100 rpm, a ratio of 15. One pair could do it, with a 10-tooth driver and a 150-tooth gear, but that big gear would be fifteen times as wide as the small one and the housing would have to be wider still.

A compound train gets the same ratio from two small pairs. The first pair's driven gear and the second pair's driver sit on the same shaft, so they are locked together and turn at the same speed. The first pair slows the speed by its ratio, and the second pair slows the result again.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the first pair has a ratio of 36 ÷ 12 = 3, which takes 1,500 rpm down to 500 rpm. The second has a ratio of 50 ÷ 10 = 5, which takes 500 rpm down to 100 rpm. The two ratios multiply: 3 × 5 = 15, and 1,500 ÷ 15 = 100 rpm. The torque rises by the same overall factor, from 4 N·m to 60 N·m. The largest gear in this box has 50 teeth, where one pair for the same ratio would need 150.

lead.text: Treat each pair as its own step. Find what it does to the speed, then hand that speed to the next pair.

lesson.orientation: Follow the turning from the pedals of a bicycle to its back wheel, and use tooth counts to find speed, torque and direction.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Halfway up a steep hill you drop the bike into its lowest gear. The pedals go light, and your legs spin fast while the bike creeps forward. At the top you shift the other way. Now each push on a pedal is hard work, but one turn of the pedals carries you a long way down the road.

Nothing about you changed in between. All you changed was which pair of toothed wheels connects your feet to the back wheel. Last lesson a lever let a small force move a heavy load by moving through a longer distance. Gears do the same job for something that turns, and the trade is between how fast it spins and how hard it pushes.

This lesson follows the turning from the pedals to the back wheel. It starts with what two gears fix between them, then asks what happens to the push. After that it adds a third gear in the middle, a bicycle chain and two pairs of gears working together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out how fast and how hard the last wheel in a train of gears turns.

recap.keyIdea: Meshing gears pass teeth at the same rate, so speed × teeth is equal on both. An ideal mesh keeps the power, so torque rises by the ratio that speed falls.

blocks.text: You followed the turning from the pedals to the back wheel. A 20-tooth driver at 1,200 rpm turns a 60-tooth gear at 400 rpm, and the torque on that gear is three times the driver's. A chain obeys the same rule as a mesh and keeps the direction, while an idler turns the output the right way round and leaves the ratio alone.

In a compound train the ratios multiply, so two 3 : 1 pairs turn 1,800 rpm into 200 rpm in a box far smaller than one 9 : 1 pair would need. The bike is a train of gears with a chain in it, and shifting gear changes the ratio.

recap.nextHook: A real gearbox runs warm, because the teeth rub as they slide past each other and some of the energy turns into heat. The next lesson works out how much of the motor's effort reaches the last gear, and what that means for the size of motor you need.

questions.prompt: How fast, in rpm, does the second gear turn?
hints: Both gears have the same number of teeth.
Teeth pass the contact point at the same rate on both gears.
Equal gears turn at equal speeds.
questions.onCorrect: 100 rpm. Same teeth, same speed. Next: what if the teeth differ?

misconceptions.feedback: Neither gear can turn faster than the other when their teeth match.
Nothing slows the second gear. Gears with equal teeth turn at equal rates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal gears pass teeth at the same rate, so both turn at 100 rpm.

questions.prompt: A 10-tooth driver meshes with a 40-tooth gear. How does the 40-tooth gear turn?
hints: Speed × teeth is equal on both gears. Which has more teeth?
questions.onCorrect: The gear with more teeth turns more slowly: speed × teeth stays equal.

misconceptions.feedback: A gear with more teeth passes more teeth per turn, so it needs fewer turns to keep pace.
Equal speeds need equal teeth. These gears have different counts.

choices.label: At the same speed as the driver

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More slowly than the driver. More teeth means fewer turns, so the 40-tooth gear turns more slowly.

questions.prompt: A 20-tooth driver gear turning at 1,200 rpm meshes with a 60-tooth gear. Find the output speed in rpm.
hints: Speed × teeth is equal on both gears.
The bigger gear turns more slowly.
Calculate 1,200 × 20 ÷ 60.
questions.onCorrect: 400 rpm: speed × teeth is equal, so three times the teeth means a third of the speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the ratio, which speeds the larger gear up. The larger gear turns more slowly.
That is the driver's speed. The gears have different teeth, so their speeds differ.

questions.prompt: A gear pair cuts a shaft's speed to a fifth. By what factor is the torque multiplied, if the mesh is lossless?
hints: An ideal mesh passes on all the power.
Power is torque times speed.
If speed falls by a factor, torque rises by the same factor.
questions.onCorrect: Five. Power is kept, so a fifth of the speed gives five times the torque.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed factor. Torque rises by the factor that speed falls by.
That squares the factor. Torque rises by the same factor as the speed falls.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Power = torque × speed is kept, so torque rises by the factor that speed falls: 5.

questions.prompt: Why does the torque rise when the speed falls?
hints: What stays the same across a lossless mesh?
questions.onCorrect: Power is kept, so a slower shaft must carry proportionally more torque.

misconceptions.feedback: Weight is not the reason. The mesh conserves power, and power is torque times speed.
Teeth transfer torque. They do not create any.

choices.label: Power is torque × speed, and an ideal mesh keeps the power.

acceptedIdeas: Power is torque × speed, and an ideal mesh keeps the power.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Power is torque × speed, and an ideal mesh keeps the power.. Power is torque times speed and is kept, so slower means more torque.

questions.prompt: Find the output torque in N·m.
hints: Torque rises by the gear ratio.
What is the ratio of driven teeth to driver teeth?
Multiply the input torque by that ratio.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Torque rises by the ratio 60/20 = 3: 10 × 3 = 30 N·m.

questions.onCorrect: 30 N·m: a third of the speed means three times the torque.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the ratio. Torque rises as speed falls.
That is the input torque. A slower output shaft carries more.

questions.prompt: A 30-tooth idler is placed between the 20-tooth driver, turning at 1,200 rpm, and the 60-tooth output. Find the idler's speed in rpm.
hints: The idler is driven directly by the 20-tooth gear.
Speed × teeth is equal across that mesh.
Calculate 1,200 × 20 ÷ 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The idler meshes with the driver: 1,200 × 20 ÷ 30 = 800 rpm. The output still turns at 1,200 × 20 ÷ 60 = 400 rpm.

questions.onCorrect: 800 rpm: the idler follows the usual rule across its own mesh with the driver.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the output gear's speed. The idler is driven by the 20-tooth gear.

questions.prompt: A compound train has 15 teeth driving 45, then, on the same shaft, 20 teeth driving 60. The input turns at 1,800 rpm. Find the output speed in rpm.
hints: Find each stage's ratio, driven over driver.
Multiply the stage ratios for a compound train.
Calculate 1,800 ÷ (3 × 3).
questions.onCorrect: 200 rpm: stage ratios multiply, so two 3 : 1 stages give 9 : 1 in a small box.

misconceptions.feedback: That applies only one stage. A compound train has two, and the ratios multiply.

questions.prompt: A bicycle's 48-tooth chainring drives a 16-tooth rear sprocket. The pedals turn at 60 rpm. Find the rear wheel's speed in rpm.
hints: The chain carries teeth past both sprockets at the same rate.
Speed × teeth is equal on both.
Calculate 60 × 48 ÷ 16.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A chain works like a mesh: 60 × 48 ÷ 16 = 180 rpm. Here the smaller sprocket is driven, so it turns faster.

questions.onCorrect: 180 rpm: the driven sprocket has fewer teeth, so it turns faster.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the ratio. The driven sprocket is the smaller one, so it turns faster.

questions.prompt: A 20-tooth driver turns a 60-tooth output through a 30-tooth idler. Compared with the driver, which way does the output turn: same or opposite?
hints: Each pair of meshing external gears turns in opposite senses. Count the meshes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same way: each external mesh reverses rotation, and there are two meshes.

questions.onCorrect: Two meshes, so two reversals: the output turns the same way as the driver.

misconceptions.feedback: Count the meshes. The idler meshes with both the driver and the output, and each mesh reverses the rotation.

questions.prompt: A 15-tooth driver supplies 6 N·m to a 45-tooth gear through a lossless mesh. Find the output torque in N·m.
hints: Find the gear ratio, driven over driver.
Torque rises by the ratio.
Calculate 6 × 45 ÷ 15.
questions.onCorrect: 18 N·m: torque rises by the gear ratio when speed falls by it.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the ratio. Torque rises as speed falls.
That is the input torque. A slower output shaft carries more.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ratio is 45/15 = 3, so the torque is 6 × 3 = 18 N·m.
